Surah Al ʿImran (Al-ʿImran), Medinan

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Maʿalim al-Tanzil) on Surah 3, verses 1–3:

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah﴾. Al-Kalbi, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas and others said: These verses were revealed concerning the delegation of Najran. They were sixty riders who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and among them were fourteen men from their nobles. Among the fourteen were three men to whom their affairs returned: al-ʿAqib, the commander of the people and the one who advised them, whom they did not depart from except by his opinion, and his name was ʿAbd al-Masih; al-Sayyid, their caretaker (thimal) and the owner of their baggage, whose name was al-Ayham; and Abu Haritha ibn ʿAlqama, their bishop (usquf) and scholar (hibr).

They entered the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he had prayed the afternoon prayer, wearing striped Yemeni garments (al-hibarat), robes and mantles, of the type of the men of Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb. Whoever saw them said: "We have never seen a delegation like them." When their prayer time came, they stood to pray in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Leave them." So they prayed facing east. Then al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib spoke with him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Submit (aslima)." They said: "We submitted before you." He said: "You lie. What prevents you from Islam is your claim that Allah has a son, your worship of the cross, and your eating of pork." They said: "If ʿIsa is not the son of Allah, then who is his father?" They all disputed with him concerning ʿIsa. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Do you not know that there is no child except that it resembles its father?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that our Lord is Qayyum (Sustainer) over everything, He preserves it and provides for it?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Does ʿIsa possess any of that?" They said: "No." He said: "Do you not know that nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Does ʿIsa know any of that except what he was taught?" They said: "No." He said: "Indeed our Lord fashioned ʿIsa in the womb however He willed, and our Lord is not of a form, and there is none like Him, and our Lord does not eat or drink." They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that ʿIsa's mother carried him as a woman carries, then delivered him as a woman delivers her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, then he ate, drank, and excreted?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then how can this be as you claim?" They fell silent. So Allah, the Exalted, revealed the beginning of Surah Al ʿImran up to about eighty-odd verses of it. [Narrated by Ibn Ishaq in al-Sira: 2/45–46 of Ibn Hisham's Sira, and al-Tabari in al-Tafsir: 6/151–153; al-Suyuti also attributed it to Ibn al-Mundhir from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, see al-Durr al-Manthur 2/141–142.]

Then the One of Might, who speaks, said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah﴾. The mim is open (mafatuh al-mim) and connected according to the common reading. The opening of the mim is only because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa al-sakinayn); it was vocalized with the lightest vowel. Abu Yusuf and Yaʿqub ibn Khalifa al-Aʿsha, from Abu Bakr, read ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah﴾ detached (maqtuʿan), with the mim unvocalized, on the intention of pausing (niyyat al-waqf), then they cut the hamza for the beginning, and treated it according to the dialect of those who cut the alif of connection (alif al-wasl).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah﴾ is a beginning (mubtada'), and what follows it is the predicate (khabar), and al-Hayy al-Qayyum is an attribute (naʿt) of Him.

﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿in truth﴾, with sincerity, ﴿confirming what is before it﴾, meaning the previous books in tawhid, the prophethoods, the reports and some of the laws. ﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before﴾. He said "sent down" (anzal) for the Torah and the Gospel because they were sent down all at once, and He said "sent down" (nazzal) for the Qur'an because it was sent down in parts, and tanzil is for multiplicity. As for "Torah" (al-tawrah), the Basrans said: its origin is wawriyah on the pattern of fawʿalah, like dawhalah and hawqalah, so the first waw was changed to ta and the open ya was made alif, becoming tawrah; then it was written with ya according to the root of the word. The Kufans said: its origin is tafʿilah, like tawsiyah and tawfiyah, so the ya was changed to alif according to the dialect of Tayy, for they say for the jariyah (girl) jaraah, and for tawsiyah tawsaah. Its root is from their saying: wara al-zand (the fire-stick produced fire) when its fire came out, and awraytuhu (I produced it). Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you considered the fire which you kindle?﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 71]. So it was named tawrah because it is light and illumination. Allah, the Exalted, said: "and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing" [al-Anbiya: 48]. It was also said that it is from al-tawriya, which is concealing the secret and alluding to something else, and most of the Torah was allusions without explicit statement.

As for "Gospel" (al-injil): it is on the pattern of ifʿil, from al-najl, which is coming out; from it the child is called najl because of his emergence. The Gospel was named thus because Allah, the Exalted, brought forth through it truth that had been effaced and obliterated. It is also said that it is from al-najal, which is the width of the eye, and it was named so because it was sent down as width and light for them. It was also said: in Hebrew the Torah is "tur," and tur means the law (shariʿah), and the Gospel in Syriac is "anqliyun," and its meaning is the crown (iklil).

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 4–6:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾, meaning a guide for whoever follows it, and it is not dual (*yuthanna*) because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*, the verbal noun form). ﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾, meaning that which distinguishes (*al-mufarriq*) between truth and falsehood. Al-Suddi said: there is an inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the verse, and its intended meaning is: "He sent down the Torah, the Gospel and the Criterion as a guidance for mankind."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Exalted in Might, the Possessor of Retribution﴾.

﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾, male or female, white or black, beautiful or ugly, complete or deficient. ﴿There is no deity except Him, the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. This was said in refutation of the delegation of Najran from the Christians, when they said: "Jesus is the son of Allah." It is as if He is saying: "How could there be a son for Allah when Allah Himself has formed him in the womb?"

We were informed by Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi, who said: we were informed by Abu Muhammad Abd al-Rahim ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Ansari, who said: Abu al-Qasim Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Baghawi told us, who said: Ali ibn al-Ja'd told us, who said: Abu Khaythama Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiya told us, from al-A'mash, from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: I heard Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us, and he was the truthful one whose word is confirmed: "Indeed, the creation of each one of you is gathered in the belly of his mother for forty days as a drop (*nutfa*), then he becomes a clot (*alaqa*) like that, [53/a] then he becomes a lump of flesh (*mudgha*) like that. Then Allah sends the angel to him" or he said: "the angel is sent to him with four words, and he writes his provision, his deeds, his term of life, and whether he is wretched or happy." He said: "Indeed, one of you may act with the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is between him and it only the length of a forearm, and then the Decree overtakes him, and he acts with the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. And indeed, one of you may act with the deeds of the people of the Fire until there is between him and it only the length of a forearm, and then the Decree overtakes him, and he acts with the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it."

[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of the Beginning of Creation, chapter "Mention of the Angels" (6/303), and in the Book of the Prophets and in the Book of Divine Decree; and by Muslim in the Book of Divine Decree, chapter "On the manner of the creation of the human being in his mother's belly...", no. (2643), 4/2036–2037; and the author in Sharh al-Sunna (1/128–129).]

We were informed by Isma'il ibn Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, who said: Abd al-Ghafir ibn Muhammad al-Farisi told us, who said: Abu Ahmad ibn Isa al-Juludi told us, who said: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Sufyan told us, who said: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj told us, who said: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Numayr told us, who said: Sufyan ibn Uyayna narrated to us, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Abu al-Tufayl, from Hudhayfa ibn Usayd, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The angel enters upon the drop after it has settled in the womb for forty or forty-five nights, and says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy?' and that is written. Then he says: 'O Lord, is it male or female?' and both are written. Its deeds, its term of life and its provision are written, then the scrolls are rolled up, and nothing is added to them or subtracted from them."

[Narrated by Muslim in the Book of Divine Decree, chapter "On the manner of the creation of the human being in his mother's belly...", no. (2644), 4/37.]

We were informed by Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi, who said: we were informed by Abu Muhammad Abd al-Rahim ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Ansari, who said: Abu al-Qasim Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Baghawi told us, who said: Ali ibn al-Ja'd told us, who said: Abu Khaythama Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiya told us, from al-A'mash, from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: I heard Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us, and he was the truthful one whose word is confirmed: "Indeed, the creation of each one of you is gathered in the belly of his mother for forty days as a drop (*nutfa*), then he becomes a clot (*alaqa*) like that, [53/a] then he becomes a lump of flesh (*mudgha*) like that. Then Allah sends the angel to him" or he said: "the angel is sent to him with four words, and he writes his provision, his deeds, his term of life, and whether he is wretched or happy." He said: "Indeed, one of you may act with the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is between him and it only the length of a forearm, and then the Decree overtakes him, and he acts with the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. And indeed, one of you may act with the deeds of the people of the Fire until there is between him and it only the length of a forearm, and then the Decree overtakes him, and he acts with the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it."

[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of the Beginning of Creation, chapter "Mention of the Angels" (6/303), and in the Book of the Prophets and in the Book of Divine Decree; and by Muslim in the Book of Divine Decree, chapter "On the manner of the creation of the human being in his mother's belly...", no. (2643), 4/2036–2037; and the author in Sharh al-Sunna (1/128–129).]

We were informed by Isma'il ibn Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, who said: Abd al-Ghafir ibn Muhammad al-Farisi told us, who said: Abu Ahmad ibn Isa al-Juludi told us, who said: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Sufyan told us, who said: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj told us, who said: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Numayr told us, who said: Sufyan ibn Uyayna narrated to us, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Abu al-Tufayl, from Hudhayfa ibn Usayd, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The angel enters upon the drop after it has settled in the womb for forty or forty-five nights, and says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy?' and that is written. Then he says: 'O Lord, is it male or female?' and both are written. Its deeds, its term of life and its provision are written, then the scrolls are rolled up, and nothing is added to them or subtracted from them."

[Narrated by Muslim in the Book of Divine Decree, chapter "On the manner of the creation of the human being in his mother's belly...", no. (2644), 4/37.]

**Al-Baghawi, *Ma'alim al-Tanzil*, on Surah Al 'Imran, verse 7**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definite (muhkamat)﴾, clear and explained in detail. They are called *muhkamat* from *ihkam* (making firm), as if He made them firm and prevented creation from altering them, because of their manifestness and the clarity of their meaning. ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾, that is, its foundation, on which rulings are based. He said ﴿they are the mother of the Book﴾ and did not say "mothers of the Book" because all the verses, in their completeness and unity, are like a single verse, and the speech of Allah is one. It is also said that its meaning is: every verse among them is the mother of the Book, as He said: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾ (23:50), meaning each of them is a sign. ﴿And others﴾ is the plural of *ukhra* (other). It is not declined (with tanwin) because it is *ma'dul* (formed by deviation) from *al-akhar*, like *'Umar* and *Zufar*. ﴿Ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾.

If it is asked: how does He here distinguish between the *muhkam* and the *mutashabih*, when elsewhere He made the whole Qur'an *muhkam*? He says: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ (11:1), and He made all of it *mutashabih* in another place, saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent with itself, [in another place]﴾ (39:23).

It has been said: where He made the whole *muhkam*, He meant that the whole is true, with no idle play or frivolity in it; and where He made the whole *mutashabih*, He meant that part of it resembles part in truth, truthfulness and beauty. Here He made part of it *muhkam* and part *mutashabih*.

The scholars differed concerning them. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: the *muhkamat* are the three verses in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ (6:151), and their counterpart in Bani Isra'il: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ (17:23), and the verses that follow. And he also said: the *mutashabihat* are the disjointed letters (*huruf al-tahajji*) at the beginnings of the surahs.

Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: the *muhkam* is what contains the lawful and the unlawful; everything else is *mutashabih*, one part resembling another in truth and confirming another, as in His saying: ﴿He leads astray thereby only the defiantly disobedient﴾ (2:26), and ﴿He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾ (10:100).

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: the *muhkam* is the *nasikh* (abrogating verse) which is acted upon, and the *mutashabih* is the *mansukh* (abrogated verse) which is believed in but not acted upon. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: the *muhkamat* of the Qur'an are its abrogating verses, its lawful and unlawful matters, its limits and obligations, and what is believed in and acted upon; the *mutashabihat* are its abrogated verses, its preceding and following parts, its parables, its oaths, and what is believed in but not acted upon.

It is also said: the *muhkamat* are what Allah made the creation able to understand, and the *mutashabih* is what Allah has kept exclusively to His knowledge, so that no one has a way to know it, such as the reports about the signs of the Hour: the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), the rising of the sun from its west, the establishment of the Hour and the ending of this world.

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: the *muhkam* is what admits of only one interpretation, and the *mutashabih* is what admits of several.

It has also been said: the *muhkam* is what its meaning is known, its proofs are clear and its evidences are manifest and do not become confused; and the *mutashabih* is what its knowledge is attained through reflection, and the common people do not recognise the distinction between truth and falsehood in it. Some of them said: the *muhkam* is what is self-sufficient in meaning, and the *mutashabih* is what is not self-sufficient except when referred to something else.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, in the narration of Badhan: the *mutashabih* is the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs. The reason is that a group of Jews, among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and their counterparts, came to the Prophet ﷺ, and Huyayy said to him: "We have been told that ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ was sent down to you. We adjure you by Allah: was it sent down to you?" He said: "Yes." He said: "If that is true, I know the length of your community's rule: it is seventy-one years. Has anything else been sent down besides this?" He said: "Yes, ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾." He said: "This is more: it is one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything else?" He said: "Yes, ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾." He said: "This is more: it is two hundred and seventy-one years. You have confused us; we do not know whether to take from its much or from its little, and we are among those who do not believe in this." Then Allah sent down: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definite, they are the mother of the Book, and others that are ambiguous﴾.
[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his *Tafsir* at length (1/216–218). al-Suyuti said in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (1/57): it was narrated by Ibn Ishaq, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, and Ibn Jarir with a weak chain. Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his *Tafsir* (1/76) and said: this hadith revolves around Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, who is among those whose singly narrated reports are not used as proof. See the annotation of Shaykh Mahmud Muhammad Shakir on al-Tabari's *Tafsir* (1/218–220).]]

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, that is, inclination away from the truth; it is also said: doubt. ﴿they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾. The scholars differed about who is meant by this verse. Al-Rabi' said: they are the delegation of Najran, who disputed with the Prophet ﷺ about 'Isa (peace be upon him). They said to him: "Do you not claim that he is the Word of Allah and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Indeed." They said: "That is enough for us." So Allah sent down this verse.

Al-Kalbi said: they are the Jews, who sought to know the term of this community and to extract it by the reckoning of *al-jumal* (the abjad numerical system). Ibn Juraij said: they are the hypocrites. Al-Hasan said: they are the Khawarij. Qatadah, when he recited this verse, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, would say: "If they are not the Harurites and the Sabaites, then I do not know who they are." It is also said: they are all the innovators (*mubtadi'ah*).

We were informed by 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi, who said: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, who said: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, who said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Maslamah informed us, who said: Yazid ibn Ibrahim al-Tustari informed us, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse, ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definite, they are the mother of the Book, and others that are ambiguous﴾, up to His saying ﴿those of understanding﴾. She said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you see those who follow that of it which is ambiguous, those are the ones whom Allah has named, so beware of them."
[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in *Tafsir*, in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran, chapter "Among it are verses that are definite" (8/209); by Muslim in *al-'Ilm*, chapter "The prohibition of following the ambiguous parts of the Qur'an and warning against those who follow them," no. 2665 (4/2053); and by the author in *Sharh al-Sunnah* (1/220–221).]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿seeking discord﴾, that is, seeking *shirk*, as said by al-Rabi' and al-Suddi. Mujahid said: seeking doubts and confusion, so that they may mislead their ignorant ones thereby. ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾, that is, its explanation and knowledge. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not be patient﴾ (18:78). It is also said: seeking its outcome, and this is seeking the term of this community from the reckoning of *al-jumal*. The evidence is His saying: ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wil)﴾ (17:35), meaning in outcome.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾. The scholars differed concerning the construction of this verse. A group said: the *waw* in His saying "and those firmly rooted" is the *waw* of conjunction, meaning that the interpretation of the ambiguous is known to Allah and also known to those firmly rooted in knowledge, who, along with their knowledge, ﴿say: We believe in it﴾. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Rabi'. On this view, His saying "say" is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "those firmly rooted in knowledge, saying: We believe in it." This is like His saying: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the townships belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives﴾ (59:7), then He said: ﴿for the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes﴾ (59:8), up to His saying: ﴿and those who had established themselves in the abode and in faith before them﴾ (59:9), then He said: ﴿and those who came after them﴾ (59:10), which is a conjunction with what precedes, then He said: ﴿saying: Our Lord, forgive us﴾ (59:10), meaning: they, along with their entitlement to the spoils, say "Our Lord, forgive us", that is, saying so as a circumstantial clause.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he used to say concerning this verse: "I am among those firmly rooted in knowledge." And it is narrated from Mujahid: "I am among those who know its interpretation."

Most scholars held that the *waw* in His saying "and those firmly rooted" is the *waw* of resumption (*istinaf*), and that the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾. This is the saying of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'A'ishah and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them), and a narration of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It was also the view of al-Hasan and most of the Successors, and al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash chose it. They said: none knows the interpretation of the ambiguous except Allah. It is possible that the Qur'an has an interpretation which Allah has kept exclusively to His knowledge and has not revealed to any of His creation, just as He kept exclusively the knowledge of the Hour, the time of the rising of the sun from its west, the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa (peace and blessings be upon him), and the like. Creation is bound by worship in the ambiguous through belief in it, and in the definite through belief in it and action. Among what confirms this is the reading of 'Abd Allah: "Indeed its interpretation is only with Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." In the codex of Ubayy: "and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it."

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said concerning this verse: the knowledge of those firmly rooted in knowledge of the interpretation of the Qur'an ends at their saying "We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord." This view is more analogical in Arabic grammar and closer to the apparent meaning of the verse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾, that is, those who go deep into knowledge; they are those who have mastered their knowledge such that no doubt enters into their understanding. Its root is from the settling (*rusukh*) of a thing in another thing, which is its becoming fixed. It is said: faith settled (*rasakha*) in the heart of so-and-so, yarsukh, *ruskh* and *rusukh*. It is also said: those firmly rooted in knowledge are the learned believers among the People of the Book, like 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. The evidence is His saying: ﴿But those firmly rooted in knowledge among them﴾ (4:162), meaning those (*al-mudarisin*) who study the knowledge of the Torah. Malik ibn Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about those firmly rooted in knowledge, and he said: the scholar who acts upon what he knows and follows it. It is also said: whoever is found to have four things in his knowledge is firmly rooted in knowledge: piety between him and Allah, humility between him and the creation, asceticism between him and the world, and striving between him and his own self.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), Mujahid and al-Suddi said: by their saying "We believe in it" Allah named them firmly rooted in knowledge; so their firmness in knowledge is their saying "We believe in it", that is, in the ambiguous. ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾: the definite and the ambiguous, the abrogating and the abrogated, what we know and what we do not know. ﴿And none takes heed﴾, that is, none is admonished by what is in the Qur'an, ﴿except the people of understanding﴾, those possessed of intellects.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 8:

God's words, ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate﴾, meaning: and those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate," i.e., do not incline them away from the truth and guidance, as You caused the hearts of those in whose hearts is deviation to deviate. ﴿After You have guided us﴾, i.e., granted us success in Your religion and in faith in the muhkam (clear) and the mutashabih (ambiguous) of Your Book. ﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾, i.e., give us from Your presence, ﴿mercy﴾, meaning success and steadfastness in what we are upon of faith and guidance. Al-Dahhak said: it means forgiveness and pardon. ﴿Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾.

Abu al-Faraj al-Muzaffar ibn Isma'il al-Tamimi informed us: Abu al-Qasim Hamza ibn Yusuf al-Sahmi related to us: Abu Ahmad ibn 'Adi al-Hafiz related to us: Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim al-Qurashi, known as Ibn al-Rawwas al-Kabir, in Damascus, related to us: Abu Musahir 'Abd al-A'la ibn Musahir al-Ghassani related to us: Sadaqah related to us: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Jabir related to us: Bishr ibn 'Ubayd Allah told me, saying: I heard Abu Idris al-Khawlani say: al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an al-Kilabi told me, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no heart but that it is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful: if He wills to set it upright, He sets it upright, and if He wills to make it deviate, He makes it deviate." And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "O Turner of the hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your religion." And "the scale is in the hand of the Most Merciful; He raises some people and lowers others, until the Day of Resurrection." [[Narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad from al-Nawwas: 4/182, and Ibn Majah in the Introduction, chapter on what the Jahmiyyah denied: 1/72, and he said in al-Zawa'id: its chain is sound. The author also cited it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 1/166.]]

Abu Ahmad ... [see note]

Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Salihi informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Hiri related to us: Hajib ibn Ahmad al-Tusi informed us: 'Abd al-Rahim ibn Munib informed us: Yazid ibn Harun informed us: Sa'id ibn Iyas al-Jurayri informed us, from Ghunaym ibn Qays, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the heart is that of a feather in an open desert, which the winds turn over, back and front." [[Narrated by Ibn Majah in the Introduction, no. (88), 1/34, and Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad: 4/408, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari with a sound chain; the author also cited it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 1/164.]]

"Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt." (Q. 3:9) That is, for the judgment of a Day. It was also said that the lam here means "in," i.e., "on a Day," ﴿in which there is no doubt﴾, meaning there is no uncertainty about it, and it is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾ Al-mi'ad is on the pattern of mif'al, derived from the root for promise (wa'd).

"Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all." (Q. 3:10) That is, they will not benefit them nor ward off anything for them. Al-Kalbi said: "from the punishment of Allah." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" here means "'inda" (with/before), i.e., before Allah. ﴿And those are the fuel of the Fire.﴾

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: like the conduct and practice of the people of Pharaoh in disbelief and denial. 'Ata', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: like the way (sunnah) of the people of Pharaoh. al-Akhfash said: like the affair and circumstance of the people of Pharaoh. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: like the habit of the people of Pharaoh, meaning the habit of these disbelievers in denying the Messenger and rejecting the truth, like the habit of the people of Pharaoh. ﴿And those before them﴾, the disbelievers of earlier nations, such as 'Ad and Thamud and others, ﴿denied Our signs, so Allah seized them﴾, that is, Allah punished them ﴿for their sins.﴾ It was also said that the wording of the verse is: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them," at the arrival of retribution and punishment, like the people of Pharaoh and the disbelievers of the past nations; We seized them, so their wealth and children did not avail them. ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

"Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and it is an evil resting-place." (Q. 3:12) Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read both verbs with ya' (yughlabuna and yuhsharuna), meaning they will be overcome and gathered; the others read both with ta' (tughlabuna and tuhsharuna), in the second person, meaning: say to them, "You will be overcome and gathered." Muqatil said: it refers to the polytheists of Makkah; the meaning is: say to the disbelievers of Makkah, "You will be overcome on the Day of Badr, and gathered to Hell in the Hereafter." When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them on the Day of Badr: "Indeed, Allah will overcome you and gather you to Hell." [Narrated by Ibn Hisham in al-Sirah from Ibn Ishaq: 2/120, and al-Tabari in al-Tafsir: 6/227 and in al-Tarikh: 2/479.]

Some of them said the verse refers to the Jews. Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): the Jews of Madinah said when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) defeated the polytheists at Badr: "This, by Allah, is the Prophet whom Musa gave us good tidings of; his banner is not turned back." They wanted to follow him, but then some of them said to others: "Do not hasten until you see another encounter." When the Day of Uhud came and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were afflicted, they doubted, and wretchedness overcame them, so they did not embrace Islam. There had been a treaty between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a set period, but they broke that treaty, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with sixty riders to Makkah to incite them, and they resolved together to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse concerning them.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from his informants, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Quraysh at Badr and returned to Madinah, he gathered the Jews in the market of Banu Qaynuqa' and said: "O assembly of Jews, beware of Allah lest there befall you the like of what befell Quraysh at Badr, and embrace Islam before there befalls you the like of what befell them. You know that I am a sent Prophet; you find this in your Book." They said: "O Muhammad, do not let it deceive you that you met a people who were inexperienced in war and so you gained an advantage over them. By Allah, if we fought you, you would know that we are the (true) men." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ [Narrated by Ibn Hisham in al-Sirah from Ibn Ishaq: 2/120, and al-Tabari in al-Tafsir: 6/227 and in al-Tarikh: 2/479.] that is, defeated, ﴿and gathered﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿to Hell﴾ ﴿and it is an evil resting-place﴾: the bed, meaning the evil thing prepared for them, namely the Fire.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There has already been for you a sign﴾, and He did not say "qad kanat lakum" (feminine). The word "āya" (sign) is feminine, but He referred it to "bayān" (clear evidence), meaning: "there has already been for you a clear proof." So He went according to the meaning.

Al-Farra' said: It was masculine only because the adjective came between the verb and the feminine noun, so the verb was made masculine. Everything that comes in this manner follows this pattern. The meaning of the verse is: "There has already been for you a sign," i.e., a lesson and an indication of the truth of what I say, that you will be victorious.

﴿In two groups﴾, two companies. The original of "fi'a" is from "fay' al-harb" (the turning back in war), because some of them return (yafi'u) to others. ﴿That met﴾ on the day of Badr. ﴿One group fighting in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., obedience to Allah, and they were the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. They numbered three hundred and thirteen men: seventy-seven men from the Muhajirun, and two hundred and thirty-six from the Ansar. The bearer of the banner of the Muhajirun was ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), and the bearer of the banner of the Ansar was Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah. Among them were seventy camels and two horses: a horse for al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr and a horse for Marthad ibn Abi Marthad. Most of them were on foot. With them were six coats of mail and eight swords.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And another, disbelieving﴾, i.e., another group disbelieving, and they were the polytheists of Makkah. They numbered nine hundred and fifty fighting men, their leader being ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah ibn ʿAbd Shams, and among them were one hundred horses. The battle of Badr was the first battlefield that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) witnessed. ﴿They saw them as twice their number﴾. The people of Madinah and Yaʿqub read it with a "ta'" (tarawna), meaning: "You see, O company of Jews, the people of Makkah as twice the Muslims." This is because a group of Jews had attended the fighting of Badr to see on whom the turn of fortune would fall, and they saw the polytheists as twice the number of the Muslims, and they saw that the support was nevertheless for the Muslims, so that was a miracle and a sign.

The others read it with a "ya'" (yarawnahum), and they differed regarding its interpretation. Some of them made the seeing belong to the Muslims, and then it has two interpretations. The first: the Muslims see the polytheists as twice themselves as they are. If it is said: how did He say "mithlayhim" (twice them) when they were three times as many? It is said: this is like the saying of a man who has a dirham, "I need twice this dirham," meaning twice it in addition to itself, so it becomes three dirhams. The second interpretation, which is the most correct: the Muslims saw the polytheists as twice the number of themselves. Allah made them appear few in their eyes until they saw them as six hundred and twenty-six, then Allah made them appear few in their eyes in another state until they saw them as equal to their own number. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We looked at the polytheists and saw them doubling against us, then we looked at them and we did not see them exceeding us by even one man." Then Allah made them appear few in their eyes again, until they saw them as a small number, fewer than themselves [Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said] [[omitted from (A)]] until I said to a man beside me: "Do you see them as seventy?" He said: "I see them as a hundred."

Some said: the seeing refers to the polytheists, meaning the polytheists see the Muslims as twice themselves. Allah made the Muslims appear few in the eyes of the polytheists before the fighting, so that the polytheists would be emboldened against them and not withdraw. When they began fighting, Allah made them appear numerous in the eyes of the polytheists so that they would become cowardly, and He made them appear few in the eyes of the believers so that they would be emboldened. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you few in their eyes﴾ (8:44, al-Anfal).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The sight of the eye﴾, i.e., in the sight of the eye. It is in the accusative by the removal of the particle of comparison (ka-) [i.e., "ra'y al-ʿayn" as an accusative of manner]. ﴿And Allah supports with His help whom He wills. Indeed in that﴾, which I have mentioned, ﴿is a lesson for those of vision﴾, for those of understanding. It was also said: for those who saw the two groups.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires﴾, plural of shahwah (desire), which is what the soul inclines towards, ﴿of women﴾.

He began with them because they are the snares of Satan. ﴿And children and heaped-up piles﴾, plural of qintar (a large measure of wealth). They differed concerning it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the qintar is abundant wealth, some of it piled upon other parts. Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the qintar is twelve hundred ounces (uqiyyah). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and [al-Dahhak] [[Omitted in manuscript A.]] said: it is twelve hundred mithqal. There is another narration from them both: twelve thousand dirhams, and a thousand [dinars] [[In manuscript B: dirham.]], the blood-money (diyah) of one of you. From al-Hasan: the qintar is the blood-money of one of you. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it is one hundred thousand, and one hundred mana, and one hundred ratl, and one hundred mithqal, and one hundred dirhams. Indeed, when Islam came, on the day it came there were in Makkah a hundred men who had become qantara (wealthy). Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatadah said: eighty thousand. Mujahid said: seventy thousand. From al-Suddi, he said: four thousand mithqal. Al-Hakam said: the qintar is wealth filling what lies between the heaven and the earth. Abu Nadrah said: a bull's hide filled with gold or silver.

It was named qintar from ihkam (firm making), as one says: qantartu al-shay' when I made the thing firm, and from it is named al-qantarah (the arch/bridge).

The Almighty's saying: ﴿the heaped-up﴾. Al-Dahhak said: the muhassanah (fortified), the muhkamah (firmly made). Qatadah said: it is the abundant, stacked, one piece placed upon another. Yaman said: [the buried] [[In manuscript B: al-mudqumah.]]. Al-Suddi said: the struck, the minted, until they become dirhams and dinars. [Al-Farra'] [[In manuscript A: al-Suddi.]] said: the doubled. Thus the qanatir are three and the muqantarah are nine. ﴿Of gold and silver﴾. It was said that gold was named dhahab because it goes away (yadhhabu) and does not remain, and silver because it is scattered (tanfadd), i.e., it dispersed.

﴿And the branded horses﴾. Al-khayl (horses) is a plural with no singular from its own form; its singular is faras, like al-qawm (the people) and al-nisa' (the women) and the like. Al-musawwamah: Mujahid said: they are the well-proportioned, the beautiful. 'Ikrimah said: its tasmim (branding/marking) is its beauty. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the grazing ones; one says: asama al-khayl and sawwamaha. Al-Hasan and Abu 'Ubaydah said: they are the marked by a sign (si'mah), and al-si'mah is the mark. Then some of them said: its sima (mark) is resemblance and colour, and this is the saying of Qatadah. It was also said: it is branding with fire.

﴿And the cattle﴾, plural of al-na'am, which are camels, cows and sheep, a plural with no singular from its own form. ﴿And the tillage﴾, meaning crops. ﴿That﴾ which we have mentioned ﴿is the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾, indicating that it is an enjoyment that perishes. ﴿And with Allah is the best return﴾, i.e., the place of return. In this is a discouragement from the world and an encouragement towards the Hereafter.

God Most High says: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and purified spouses, and approval from Allah."﴾ [54b] The common readers (al-'ammah) read ﴿ridwan﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ (ر), while Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim with a ḍamma on the rāʾ. Both are dialectal variants (lughatan), like ﴿al-'udwan﴾ and ﴿al-'idwan﴾ (both meaning transgression).

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Yahya ibn Sulayman informed us: Ibn Wahb narrated to me: Malik narrated to me, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' and they say: 'At Your service, our Lord, and at Your pleasure, and all good is in Your hands.' He says: 'Are you content?' They say: 'And why would we not be content, O Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He says: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They say: 'O Lord, and what could be better than that?' He says: 'I shall make My approval (riḍwan) descend upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you after it, ever.'" [Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tawhid, chapter: The Speech of the Lord with the People of Paradise, 3/487; and Muslim in Paradise, chapter: The Descent of Approval upon the People of Paradise, so that He is never displeased with them, no. 2829, 4/2176.]

God Most High says: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants.﴾

﴿Those who say﴾ (alladhina yaqulun): If you wish, you may make the position (maḥall) of ﴿alladhina﴾ genitive (khafḍan), as a reply (radd) to His words ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾. If you wish, you may make it nominative (raf'an) as the beginning of a sentence (ibtida'). It may also be accusative (naṣban), with the implied meaning: "I mean those who say..." ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed﴾ means: we have affirmed (ṣaddaqna). ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾ means: cover them over for us and overlook them for us. ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾

﴿The patient and the truthful﴾ (al-ṣabirin wal-ṣadiqin): If you wish, you may put them in the accusative as praise (nasb 'ala al-madḥ), and if you wish, you may put them in the genitive as a description (khafḍ 'ala al-na't). The meaning is: those who are patient in performing the command and in refraining from committing what is forbidden, and in adversity (al-ba'sa') and hardship (al-ḍarra') and at the time of battle (ḥina al-ba's). And the truthful in their faith. Qatadah said: "They are a people whose intentions were sincere, whose hearts and tongues were upright, so they were truthful in secret and in public." ﴿And the obedient﴾ (al-qanitin): those who are obedient and who pray. ﴿And the spenders﴾ (al-munfiqin), who spend their wealth in obedience to Allah. ﴿And those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ (al-mustaghfirin bil-asḥar): Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: "It means those who pray at the pre-dawn hours (al-asḥar)." It is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "They are those who pray the dawn prayer in congregation." It was also said: "(al-saḥar) refers to the time close to dawn." Al-Hasan said: "They extended the prayer until the pre-dawn, then sought forgiveness." Nafi' said: "Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, would stay up the night in prayer, then say: 'O Nafi', has dawn come?' I would say: 'No.' So he would resume prayer. When I said: 'Yes,' he would sit, seek forgiveness from Allah and supplicate until morning."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi informed us: Abu Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad al-Makhladi informed us: Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Sarraj informed us: Qutaybah [ibn Sa'id] [omitted in manuscript "b"] informed us: Ya'qub ibn Abd al-Rahman informed us, from Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah descends to the lowest heaven every night when a third of the night remains, and says: 'I am the King, I am the King. Who is there that calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is there that asks Me, that I may give to him? Who is there that seeks forgiveness from Me, that I may forgive him?'" [Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tahajjud, chapter: Supplication and Prayer in the Last Part of the Night, 3/29; and Muslim in the Prayer of Travellers, chapter: Encouragement to Supplication and Remembrance in the Last Part of the Night and Its Acceptance, no. 758, 1/521; and the author (al-Mu'allif) in Sharh al-Sunnah, 4/63-64.]

It is related from al-Hasan that Luqman said to his son: "O my son, do not be weaker than this rooster, which calls out at the pre-dawn hours while you are sleeping on your bed."

Qatadah said: "They are a people whose intentions were sincere, whose hearts and tongues were upright, so they were truthful in secret and in public." ﴿And the obedient﴾ (al-qanitin): those who are obedient and who pray. ﴿And the spenders﴾ (al-munfiqin), who spend their wealth in obedience to Allah. ﴿And those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ (al-mustaghfirin bil-asḥar): Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: "It means those who pray at the pre-dawn hours (al-asḥar)." It is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "They are those who pray the dawn prayer in congregation." It was also said: "(al-saḥar) refers to the time close to dawn." Al-Hasan said: "They extended the prayer until the pre-dawn, then sought forgiveness." Nafi' said: "Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, would stay up the night in prayer, then say: 'O Nafi', has dawn come?' I would say: 'No.' So he would resume prayer. When I said: 'Yes,' he would sit, seek forgiveness from Allah and supplicate until morning."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi informed us: Abu Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad al-Makhladi informed us: Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Sarraj informed us: Qutaybah [ibn Sa'id] [omitted in manuscript "b"] informed us: Ya'qub ibn Abd al-Rahman informed us, from Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah descends to the lowest heaven every night when a third of the night remains, and says: 'I am the King, I am the King. Who is there that calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is there that asks Me, that I may give to him? Who is there that seeks forgiveness from Me, that I may forgive him?'" [Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tahajjud, chapter: Supplication and Prayer in the Last Part of the Night, 3/29; and Muslim in the Prayer of Travellers, chapter: Encouragement to Supplication and Remembrance in the Last Part of the Night and Its Acceptance, no. 758, 1/521; and the author (al-Mu'allif) in Sharh al-Sunnah, 4/63-64.]

It is related from al-Hasan that Luqman said to his son: "O my son, do not be weaker than this rooster, which calls out at the pre-dawn hours while you are sleeping on your bed."

God Most High says: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and purified spouses, and approval from Allah."﴾ [54b] The common readers (al-'ammah) read ﴿ridwan﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ (ر), while Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim with a ḍamma on the rāʾ. Both are dialectal variants (lughatan), like ﴿al-'udwan﴾ and ﴿al-'idwan﴾ (both meaning transgression).

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Yahya ibn Sulayman informed us: Ibn Wahb narrated to me: Malik narrated to me, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' and they say: 'At Your service, our Lord, and at Your pleasure, and all good is in Your hands.' He says: 'Are you content?' They say: 'And why would we not be content, O Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He says: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They say: 'O Lord, and what could be better than that?' He says: 'I shall make My approval (riḍwan) descend upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you after it, ever.'" [Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tawhid, chapter: The Speech of the Lord with the People of Paradise, 3/487; and Muslim in Paradise, chapter: The Descent of Approval upon the People of Paradise, so that He is never displeased with them, no. 2829, 4/2176.]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran. Al-Kalbi said: Two rabbis from the rabbis of Syria came to the Prophet (ﷺ). When they saw Medina, one of them said to his companion: "How much does this city resemble the description of the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) who will emerge at the end of time?" When they entered upon him, they recognized him by the description, and they said to him: "Are you Muhammad?" He said: "Yes." They said: "And are you Ahmad?" He said: "I am Muhammad and Ahmad." They said: "We will ask you about something, and if you inform us of it, we will believe in you and affirm you." He said: "Ask." They said: "Inform us about the greatest testimony in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." So Allah, Exalted, revealed this verse, and the two men embraced Islam. [[See: al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan: 2/401-402. The hadith is from the narration of al-Kalbi, who is accused of lying. See also what will come regarding the interpretation of verse (23), and Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi p. (130).]]

His saying ﴿Allah bears witness﴾: that is, Allah made clear, because testimony makes clear. Mujahid said: Allah judged [and it was said: Allah knew] [[Omitted from "b".]]. It was also said: Allah informed that there is no deity except Him.

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Allah created the spirits before the bodies by four thousand years, and He created the provisions before the spirits by four thousand years. So He bore witness for Himself to Himself before He created the creation, when there was nothing, and there was no heaven, no earth, no land, and no sea, and He said: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾. [[Scholars differ on this question: some say that Allah created the spirits first, and others say that Allah created the bodies first, and each group has evidences by which it supports its view. See: al-Ruh of Ibn al-Qayyim p. (156-175).]]

His saying: ﴿and the angels﴾: that is, the angels also bear witness. It was said: the meaning of Allah's testimony is informing and announcing, and the meaning of the testimony of the angels and the believers is affirmation. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and those of knowledge﴾: meaning the prophets, peace be upon them.

Ibn Kaysan said: meaning the Muhajirun and the Ansar. Muqatil said: the scholars among the believers of the People of the Book, Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: meaning all the scholars of the believers.

﴿Standing in justice﴾: that is, upholding justice. The structure of this verse: "Allah bears witness, standing in justice," is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it was said it is in the accusative as a restrictive/detached state (qaṭʿ). The meaning of His saying ﴿standing in justice﴾: that is, standing in the management of creation, as one says: "So-and-so stands in the affair of so-and-so," meaning he manages it and attends to its causes, and "stands in the right of so-and-so," meaning he repays him. So Allah, majestic is His majesty, is the Manager, the Provider, the Recompenser for deeds.

﴿There is no deity except Him, the Mighty, the Wise﴾

**Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam.** [Al-Baghawi:] This means the religion that is approved and correct. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ (3 - Al-Ma'idah). He also said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ (85 - Al Imran). Al-Kisa'i opened the alif of *anna* in *anna al-din* (إِنَّ الدِّينَ, "that the religion"), as a restatement (*radd*) of the *anna* in the first clause, so that the sense is: Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and He bears witness that the religion with Allah is Islam; or, Allah bears witness that the religion with Allah is Islam, by [the fact that] there is no god but He. The rest read the alif with a kasra, as a new sentence (*ibtida'*). Islam is entering into peace (*al-silm*), which is submission and obedience. It is said: *aslama*, meaning he entered into peace and *istaslama* (he surrendered). Qatadah said regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the affirmation of what has come from Allah the Exalted. It is the religion of Allah, which He legislated for Himself, sent His messengers with, and guided His friends (*awliya'*) to. [He does not accept anything other than it, and no one is rewarded except by it.]

We were informed by Abu Sa'id al-Shurayhi, who said: Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us, who said: Abu 'Amr al-Furati informed us, who said: Abu Musa 'Imran ibn Musa informed us, who said: al-Hasan ibn Sufyan informed us, who said: 'Ammar ibn 'Umar ibn al-Mukhtar informed us, who said: my father narrated to me from Ghalib al-Qattan, who said: I came to Kufa on a trade journey and stayed near al-A'mash, and I used to frequent him. One night I intended to set off for Basra, and I found al-A'mash standing in the night in prayer (*yatahajjad*). He recited this verse: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. Then al-A'mash said: "I too bear witness to what Allah has borne witness to, and I entrust Allah with this testimony, which is with Him as a deposit for me." Then he said ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ several times. I said: "He must have heard something about it." So I prayed with him and bade him farewell. Then I said: "I heard you recite a verse and repeat it. What has reached you concerning it?" [He said to me: "Has it not reached you what is in it?" I said: "I have been with you for two years and you have not related it to me."] He said: "By Allah, I will not narrate it to you until a year has passed." So I wrote at his door that day and stayed for a year. When the year had passed, I said: "O Abu Muhammad, the year has passed." He said: Abu Wa'il narrated to me from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Its companion will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will say: 'Indeed, this servant of Mine has a covenant with Me, and I am most worthy of fulfilling the covenant. Admit My servant into Paradise.'" [Al-Suyuti said: It was narrated by Ibn 'Adi, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, who declared it weak, al-Khatib in his History, and Ibn al-Najjar, from Ghalib al-Qattan. See: al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti, 2/166. Al-Haythami mentioned it in al-Majma' 6/325-326 and said: al-Tabarani narrated it, and in its chain is 'Umar ibn al-Mukhtar, who is weak. Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned several narrations for it and said: this is a hadith that is not authentic from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; 'Umar ibn al-Mukhtar is alone in it, and 'Umar narrates falsehoods. Al-'Uqayli said: no one follows 'Ammar in his hadith, and it is not known except through him. See: al-'Ilal al-Mutanahiyah fi al-Ahadith al-Wahiyah of Ibn al-Jawzi, 1/102-103; Mizan al-I'tidal of al-Dhahabi, 3/223.]

**His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾.** Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians when they abandoned Islam. That is: those given the Scripture did not differ concerning the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ except after knowledge had come to them, meaning the clarification of his description in their books. Al-Rabi' said: When Musa (peace be upon him) was near death, he summoned seventy men from the rabbis (*ahbar*) of the Children of Israel, entrusted them with the Torah, and appointed Yusha' ibn Nun as successor. When the first, second and third generations passed, division occurred among them, and they were the people of the Scripture from among the descendants of those seventy, until they shed blood among themselves, and evil and disagreement occurred. That was after knowledge had come to them, meaning the clarification of what is in the Torah. ﴿Out of envy among themselves﴾, that is, seeking kingship and leadership, so Allah gave the tyrants power over them. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran, and its meaning is: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ﴾, meaning the Gospel, concerning the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and they divided their statements about it, ﴿except after knowledge had come to them﴾ that Allah is One and that 'Isa is His servant and messenger. ﴿Out of envy among themselves﴾, that is, out of enmity and opposition. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 3, verses 20–21:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they dispute with you﴾, that is, argue with you, O Muhammad, about the religion. This is because the Jews and the Christians said: "We are not upon what you have named us, O Muhammad. Judaism and Christianity are only lineages, and the religion is Islam, and we are upon it." So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾, that is, I have surrendered to Allah alone with my heart, my tongue, and all my limbs. The face is singled out because it is the most honourable of a person's limbs and the place of his beauty. When his face submits to something, all his other limbs submit to it as well.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "I have sincerely devoted my deeds to Allah." ﴿And those who follow me﴾, that is, whoever follows me, let him submit as I have submitted.

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr kept the ya' (the final long vowel "ī") in His saying ﴿ittaba'anī﴾ ("followed me") according to the original form, while the others omitted it in accordance with the written form (al-khatt), because in the mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an) it is written without a ya'.

And His saying: ﴿Say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered ones﴾, meaning the Arabs, ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ Its wording is interrogative (istifham), but its meaning is a command, that is, "Submit!" This is like His saying: "So will you not desist?" (5:91), meaning "Desist!" ﴿And if they submit, then they are guided﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, and the People of the Book said: "We have submitted." Then he said to the Jews: "Do you testify that Jesus is the Word of Allah, His servant, and His Messenger?" They said: "God forbid!" He said to the Christians: "Do you testify that Jesus is the servant of Allah and His Messenger?" They said: "God forbid that Jesus should be a servant!" Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the conveyance (of the message)﴾, that is, the conveying of the message, and it is not upon you to guide them. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾, Knowing of who believes and who does not believe.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among the people — give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ (3:21)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, who deny the signs of Allah, meaning the Qur'an. They are the Jews and the Christians. ﴿And kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among the people﴾. Hamza recited: "wa-yuqatiluna alladhina ya'muruna" ("and fight those who enjoin"). Ibn Jurayj said: Revelation used to come to the prophets of the Children of Israel, but no book came to them. They would admonish their people and be killed. Then men would rise up from among those who followed and believed them, and they would admonish their people and be killed as well. These are the ones who enjoin justice among the people.

Abu Sa'id al-Shurayhi informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us: Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Fanjawayh al-Dinawari informed us: Abu Nasr Mansur ibn Ja'far al-Nahawandi informed us: Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn al-Jarud informed us: Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hayyan informed us: Muhammad ibn (Himyar) [[In "A" it is "Numayr," which is an error.]] informed us: Abu al-Hasan, the client of the Banu Asad, from Makhul, from Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb al-Khuza'i, from Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which of the people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "A man who killed a prophet, or a man [["Rajulan" is coordinated with "nabiyyan." In al-Tabari it reads: "or a man who commanded the wrong and forbade the right," coordinated with "rajul."]] who commanded what is right and forbade what is wrong." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And they kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among the people﴾ until he reached His saying ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu 'Ubayda, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day, in a single hour. Then a hundred and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel rose up. They commanded those who were killing them to do right and forbade them from wrong, and they (the killers) killed them all at the end of that same day. They are the ones whom Allah mentioned in His Book, and He revealed the verse concerning them." [[Recorded by al-Tabari in his Tafsir: 6/285–286. al-Suyuti attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Durr al-Manthur: 2/168. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Kafi al-Shafi: It was narrated by al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tha'labi through this narration, and in its chain is Abu al-Hasan, the client of the Banu Asad, who is unknown (majhul). See: al-Kafi al-Shafi, p. 25.]] ﴿So give them tidings﴾, inform them, ﴿of a painful punishment﴾, a grievous one. The fa' (then) was placed before the predicate of inna (indeed), and its implied structure is "Indeed, those who disbelieve and kill, so give them tidings," because one does not say: "inna Zaydan fa-qa'imun" ("indeed Zayd is so-and-so standing").

Commentary of al-Baghawi (*Ma'alim al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verses 22–23:

﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ *Batalat* (became void), *a'maluhum* (their deeds), *fi al-dunya wa al-akhirah* (in this world and the Hereafter). The nullification of deeds in this world means that they are not accepted, and in the Hereafter it means that they are not rewarded for them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ meaning the Jews, ﴿who are called to the Book of God﴾. They differed concerning this Book. Qatadah said: They are the Jews, who were called to the judgment of the Qur'an, but they turned away from it.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning this verse: Allah the Exalted made the Qur'an a judge between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Qur'an ruled against the Jews and the Christians that they were upon other than guidance, and they turned away from it. Others said: It refers to the Torah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered *Bayt al-Madaris* (the house of study) upon a group of Jews, and he invited them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: "What religion are you upon, O Muhammad?" He said: "Upon the religion of Ibrahim." They said: "Ibrahim was a Jew." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then bring the Torah; it is between us and you." But they refused him, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his *Tafsir* from Ibn 'Abbas: 6/228–229; and Ibn Shihab in *al-Sirah*: 2/201. Al-Suyuti also attributed it to Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim. See *al-Durr al-Manthur*: 2/170; *Asbab al-Nuzul*, p. 131.]]

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a man and a woman from the people of Khaybar committed adultery, and in their book the punishment was stoning. They disliked stoning them because of their nobility among them, so they referred their matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), hoping that he would have a concession. He ruled that they be stoned. Al-Nu'man ibn Awfa and Bahri ibn 'Amr said to him: "You have been unjust toward them, O Muhammad; stoning is not due for them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between me and you is the Torah." They said: "You have been fair to us." He said: "Who is the most knowledgeable of you in the Torah?" They said: "A one-eyed man who lives in Fadak, called Ibn Suriya." So they sent for him, and he came to Madinah. Jibril had described him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Are you Ibn Suriya?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Are you the most knowledgeable of the Jews?" He said: "That is what they claim." He said: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for a portion of the Torah, in which the stoning was written, and said to him: "Read." When he came to the verse of stoning, he placed his palm over it and read what came after it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: "O Messenger of Allah, he has passed over it." So he stood up, lifted his palm from it, and then read to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the Jews: that the married man and the married woman, if they commit adultery and the evidence is established against them, shall be stoned; and if the woman is pregnant, she shall be made to wait until she delivers what is in her womb. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then ordered the two Jews to be stoned, and they were stoned. The Jews were angered by this and departed, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who are called to the Book of God﴾[[The story is from the narration of al-Kalbi from Ibn 'Abbas. This al-Kalbi is Abu al-Nadr Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, who is accused of lying. When he fell ill, he said to his companions in his illness: "Everything I have narrated to you from Abu Salih is a lie." See *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*: 9/157–159; *al-Isra'iliyyat wa al-Mawdu'at fi al-Tafsir* by Shaykh Muhammad Abu Shahbah. It is, however, established that the two Jews who committed adultery were stoned in the six canonical books. See *Nasb al-Rayah* by al-Zayla'i: 3/326–327.]] ﴿so that He may judge between them; then a faction of them turns away, while they are averse.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (*Ma'alim al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verses 22–23:

﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ *Batalat* (became void), *a'maluhum* (their deeds), *fi al-dunya wa al-akhirah* (in this world and the Hereafter). The nullification of deeds in this world means that they are not accepted, and in the Hereafter it means that they are not rewarded for them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ meaning the Jews, ﴿who are called to the Book of God﴾. They differed concerning this Book. Qatadah said: They are the Jews, who were called to the judgment of the Qur'an, but they turned away from it.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning this verse: Allah the Exalted made the Qur'an a judge between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Qur'an ruled against the Jews and the Christians that they were upon other than guidance, and they turned away from it. Others said: It refers to the Torah.
